title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams track and manage their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Jira to Plane, possibly due to the core use case of issue tracking and project management, and the key reason being the desire for more control over their data and costs. Teams looking for a self-hosted solution with more flexibility may find this comparison useful.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira is a paid tool with a per-user pricing model, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to have full control over their data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Jira is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large teams and enterprises, while Plane is better suited for smaller teams and organizations.
* Integration with Git: Jira has native integration with Git, while Plane relies on third-party integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725.00/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550.00-$2,900.00/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Jira
* Easy to use and set up
* Native integration with Git and other Atlassian tools
* Scalable and reliable
* Good customer support
* Expensive for large teams
### Plane
* Free and self-hosted
* Full control over data
* Customizable and flexible
* Good for small teams and organizations
* Limited scalability and support

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams and enterprises that need a scalable and reliable project management tool. It is also a good option for teams that are already using other Atlassian tools and want native integration. Plane, on the other hand, is a good choice for small teams and organizations that want a free and self-hosted solution with full control over their data. It is also a good option for teams that are looking for a customizable and flexible tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export data from Jira in CSV or JSON format.
2. Use a third-party import tool to migrate data to Plane.
3. Configure Plane to match the team's workflow and processes.
4. Test and verify that all data has been migrated correctly.
5. Train team members on how to use Plane.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane does not have native integration with Git, which may be a deal-breaker for some teams. However, for small teams and organizations that want a free and self-hosted solution with full control over their data, Plane is a good option. Teams that do not need the scalability and reliability of Jira may find that Plane meets their needs.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of less than 10 users that do not need native Git integration
* Organizations that want a self-hosted solution with full control over their data
* Teams that are currently using Jira and are looking to reduce costs
* Development teams that want a customizable and flexible tool
* Teams that do not need the scalability and reliability of Jira

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted. However, teams will need to pay for server costs.
### Can I migrate my data from Jira to Plane?
Yes, you can export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using a third-party import tool.
### Is Plane scalable?
No, Plane is not yet scalable for large teams and enterprises. It is better suited for small teams and organizations.
### Does Plane have native integration with Git?
No, Plane does not have native integration with Git. However, it can be integrated with Git using third-party tools.
### Is Plane production-ready?
Not yet, Plane is still lacking some of the features and polish of Jira.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*

title: Linear vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Linear vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Linear and Plane are two project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Linear who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to Plane's self-hosted option and free cost. The core use case for both tools is project management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Linear offers a free plan and a paid plan at $8/user/month, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data Ownership: Plane allows teams to have full ownership of their data since it's self-hosted, whereas Linear stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, especially for self-hosting, compared to Linear's straightforward signup process.
* Scalability: Linear is designed to scale with large teams and has built-in features for this, whereas Plane's scalability depends on the server capabilities of the self-hosting team.
* Integration Difference: Linear has a more comprehensive set of integrations with third-party tools, including popular services like GitHub and Slack, while Plane has more limited integration options.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Linear | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $8/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $400/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,600/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Linear
* Easy to set up and use
* Comprehensive integration with third-party tools
* Scalable for large teams
* User-friendly interface
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Plane
* Self-hosted for full data control and security
* Free with no per-user costs
* Highly customizable
* Open-source for community contributions
* Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance

## When to Choose Each
Linear is the better choice for teams that prioritize ease of use, comprehensive integrations, and scalability without worrying about the costs associated with per-user fees. It's ideal for large teams or those who need a straightforward project management solution without delving into technical complexities. 
Plane is suitable for teams that value data ownership, security, and customization. It's perfect for smaller teams or organizations with the technical capability to self-host and maintain their project management tool, prioritizing control and cost-effectiveness over ease of use and integration breadth.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Linear in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up your Plane server according to the official documentation.
3. Use Plane's import tool to migrate your data from the exported Linear files.
4. Configure any necessary integrations or customizations in Plane.
5. Test your setup to ensure all data and functionalities are correctly migrated.

## Our Take
Plane offers a compelling alternative to Linear for teams seeking more control over their data and looking to reduce costs. However, for most users, Plane may not be production-ready due to its requirement for technical expertise and the potential for maintenance overhead. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is Plane's current lack of support for certain integrations that Linear offers, which could impact workflow for some teams. For teams prioritizing data security, customization, and cost-effectiveness, and who have the technical capabilities to support self-hosting, switching to Plane is a clear recommendation.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of less than 10 users who prioritize cost-effectiveness and data control
* Technical teams who can handle self-hosting and customization
* Organizations with strict data security requirements
* Teams not reliant on comprehensive third-party integrations
* Businesses looking for an open-source project management solution

## FAQ
### Is Plane completely free?
Yes, Plane is completely free as it's open-source and self-hosted, with no per-user costs.
### Does Plane offer the same integrations as Linear?
No, Plane currently has more limited integration options compared to Linear.
### Can I self-host Linear?
No, Linear does not offer a self-hosting option.
### How difficult is it to migrate from Linear to Plane?
The difficulty of migration depends on the complexity of your data and workflows in Linear, but Plane provides tools to import data from CSV or JSON files.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams?
While Plane can be used by large teams, its scalability and maintenance requirements may make it less ideal compared to solutions like Linear that are designed to scale with large teams.

title: Asana vs Taiga
comparison_markdown:
# Asana vs Taiga (2026)

## Overview
Asana and Taiga are project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams considering switching from Asana to Taiga, particularly those looking for a self-hosted solution with more control over their data. The core use case for both tools is task and project management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more flexibility and autonomy over their workflow.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Asana offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $10.99 per user, while Taiga is free and open-source, with optional self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Asana stores user data on its servers, while Taiga allows users to host their own instance and maintain full control over their data.
* Setup complexity: Asana has a more streamlined setup process, while Taiga requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, particularly for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Asana is designed to scale with large teams and enterprises, while Taiga is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration with Git: Taiga has native integration with Git repositories, while Asana requires third-party integrations to achieve similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Asana | Taiga |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10.99+/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $10.99 * 50 = $549.50 | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $10.99 * 200 = $2198 | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Asana:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Robust feature set, including reporting and analytics
* Integrates with many third-party tools and services
* Scalable and suitable for large teams
* Mobile apps available
* Limited customization options for workflows and fields
**Taiga:**
* Free and open-source, with optional self-hosting
* High degree of customization and control over workflows and fields
* Native integration with Git repositories
* Suitable for teams who value data ownership and autonomy
* Limited support for large teams and enterprises
* Setup and configuration can be complex

## When to Choose Each
Asana is a good choice for teams who need a streamlined, user-friendly project management tool with a robust feature set and integrations with other tools and services. It is particularly suitable for large teams and enterprises who require scalability and support. Taiga, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams who value data ownership and autonomy, and are willing to invest time and effort into setting up and customizing their workflow. It is particularly suitable for smaller to medium-sized teams who require a high degree of customization and control over their workflow.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Asana data in JSON format using the Asana API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Taiga instance, either self-hosted or using a cloud provider.
3. Use the Taiga import tool to import your Asana data, or write a custom script to map your Asana data to Taiga's data model.
4. Configure your Taiga workflow and customize your fields and workflows as needed.
5. Test your Taiga instance and ensure that all data has been imported correctly.

## Our Take
Taiga is a production-ready tool for teams who value data ownership and autonomy, but it may not be suitable for all users due to its complexity and limited support for large teams. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Taiga's self-hosted instance requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain. We recommend switching to Taiga if you are a small to medium-sized team who values customization and control over your workflow, and are willing to invest time and effort into setting up and customizing your workflow.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who require a high degree of customization and control over their workflow
* Teams who value data ownership and autonomy, and are willing to invest time and effort into setting up and customizing their workflow
* Teams who do not require integrations with other tools and services
* Teams who are comfortable with self-hosting and maintaining their own instance
* Teams who require native integration with Git repositories

## FAQ
### Can I use Taiga for free?
Yes, Taiga is free and open-source, with optional self-hosting.
### Is Asana suitable for small teams?
Yes, Asana has a free plan and is suitable for small teams, but it may not offer the same level of customization and control as Taiga.
### Can I migrate my Asana data to Taiga?
Yes, you can export your Asana data in JSON format and import it into Taiga using the Taiga import tool or a custom script.
### Does Taiga have mobile apps?
No, Taiga does not have mobile apps, but it has a responsive web interface that can be accessed on mobile devices.
### Is Taiga suitable for large teams and enterprises?
No, Taiga is not suitable for large teams and enterprises due to its limited support and scalability.

# Airtable vs NocoDB (2026)

## Overview
Airtable and NocoDB are two database management tools that help teams manage and organize their data. This comparison is beneficial for teams and individuals who are looking for a database solution that meets their specific needs, especially those considering switching from Airtable to a self-hosted alternative like NocoDB due to cost or data ownership concerns.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Airtable offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $10-$20 per user/month, while NocoDB is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: NocoDB allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Airtable's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user data.
* Setup complexity: Airtable is generally easier to set up and use, especially for non-technical users, while NocoDB requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Both tools can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but NocoDB's self-hosted nature gives users more control over scalability.
* Feature difference: Airtable has a more comprehensive set of built-in automation and integration features, while NocoDB offers more flexibility in terms of customization and extension through its open-source nature.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Airtable | NocoDB |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10-$20/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | Approximately $500-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | Approximately $2000-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Airtable
* Easy to use and set up, even for non-technical users
* Comprehensive set of built-in automation and integration features
* Scalable and reliable
* Good customer support
* Limited customization options
### NocoDB
* Self-hosted and free
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Gives users full ownership of their data
* Open-source and community-driven
* Requires more technical expertise to set up and use
* Limited built-in automation and integration features

## When to Choose Each
Airtable is a good choice for teams that need a easy-to-use, scalable, and reliable database solution with a comprehensive set of built-in features. It's especially suitable for teams that don't have the technical expertise to self-host a database and are willing to pay for the convenience. On the other hand, NocoDB is a good choice for teams that value data ownership, customization, and extensibility, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted database solution. This is especially true for larger teams or teams with specific security or compliance requirements.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Airtable in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a NocoDB instance on your server or local machine.
3. Use the NocoDB import tool to import your data from the CSV or JSON file.
4. Configure any necessary settings, such as user permissions and automation rules.
5. Test your database to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
NocoDB is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the polish and ease of use of more established solutions like Airtable. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that NocoDB's automation and integration features are not yet as comprehensive as those of Airtable. However, for teams that value data ownership, customization, and extensibility, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted database solution, NocoDB is a promising alternative to Airtable.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced automation features
* Teams with specific security or compliance requirements that require self-hosting
* Developers or technical teams that value customization and extensibility
* Teams with limited budgets that can't afford Airtable's per-user costs
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and control

## FAQ
### Can I use NocoDB for free?
Yes, NocoDB is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it without paying any subscription fees.
### Is NocoDB as easy to use as Airtable?
No, NocoDB requires more technical expertise to set up and use, especially for non-technical users.
### Can I migrate my data from Airtable to NocoDB?
Yes, you can export your data from Airtable in CSV or JSON format and import it into NocoDB.
### Does NocoDB have the same automation features as Airtable?
Not yet, NocoDB's automation and integration features are still in development and are not yet as comprehensive as those of Airtable.
### Is NocoDB suitable for large teams?
Yes, NocoDB can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but it requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain.
